title: The nod
summary_es: Ensayo filosófico: qué queremos decir cuando afirmamos que alguien —o algo— «entiende de verdad», y por qué quizá sea la pregunta equivocada.
prediction_prompt: Think of someone who passes exams by memorising. In what sense do they "not really understand"? How would you prove it?

sentences.text: At school I sat next to a boy who was, by every available measure, better at physics than I was.
He collected full marks with a regularity that the rest of us found faintly insulting.
It was only in our final year, when an examiner had the bad manners to set a question that resembled nothing in the textbook, that his secret came out.
He had never solved a problem in his life.

He had memorised several hundred solutions, together with the kinds of question that summoned each one, and he had done it so thoroughly that for six years nobody, possibly including him, had noticed the difference.
We said afterwards, with the satisfaction of the mediocre, that he had never really understood the subject.
I have been turning that verdict over ever since, because I am no longer sure what we were accusing him of lacking.
It cannot have been the right answers; he had more of those than anybody.
Nor was it speed, or confidence, or the ability to show his working, which was immaculate.
Whatever was missing, it left no trace on anything he actually produced, until the afternoon it left a trace on everything.
The obvious reply is that understanding shows itself in the unfamiliar case.
To have grasped a principle is to know how to go on: to do the right thing with a problem you have not met, in the way that someone who has learnt to add can add numbers nobody has ever shown them.
On this view my neighbour possessed a very large table and no rule, and the examiner merely asked for an entry the table did not contain.
It is a tidy account, and for most of my adult life I thought it was the whole story.
It has been unsettled, as so much has, by machines.
We now have systems that have read more than any person could read in ten thousand lifetimes and that produce, on request, a competent paragraph about almost anything.
Give them a problem they have demonstrably never seen and they will, quite often, go on correctly.
By the test I have just proposed, that ought to settle the matter in their favour.
Yet a great many thoughtful people, shown the performance, feel precisely what we felt about the boy at the next desk: that something is being imitated rather than done.
The classic way of sharpening that suspicion is a thought experiment that has been argued over for more than forty years.
Imagine a man shut in a room with an enormous book of instructions.
Slips of paper covered in unfamiliar marks are pushed under the door; he looks up the marks, copies out whatever the book dictates, and pushes the result back.
To those outside, who happen to read the language, the room is conducting a thoughtful correspondence.
The man inside is doing nothing of the sort.
He is matching shapes.
Rules, the argument concludes, however elaborate, will never add up to meaning.
I used to find this unanswerable.
I now think it proves rather less than it seems to, because it asks us to look for understanding in the one place it was never likely to be.
Nobody supposes that a single cell in my brain understands English either.
If comprehension exists anywhere in the story, it belongs to the whole arrangement and not to the clerk at its centre, whose boredom is beside the point.
What the experiment really shows is that our intuitions about understanding were formed by meeting creatures of roughly our own size and shape, and that they give out when the candidate is a room.
A more honest approach might be to admit that 'understanding' was never one thing.
When I say I understand how a bicycle stays upright, I may mean that I can ride one, or that I can explain the physics, or that I could tell you what would happen if the wheels were smaller.
These abilities come apart all the time.
Most cyclists have the first without the second; a good many physicists, I am told, have the second without the first.
My schoolfriend had a narrow, brittle version of one of them.
The machines have a broad and surprisingly flexible version of several, and still, apparently, lack something we find hard to name.
My own guess is that what we are groping for is not an ability at all but a stake.
To understand that a stove is hot is, in part, to be the kind of thing that can be burnt.
To understand a promise is to be someone who can be let down.
A great deal of what we know, we know as creatures to whom things matter, and it is not obvious that this can be supplied by further reading.
I offer this tentatively.
It may turn out to be the last refuge of a species unused to competition, and I am aware that every previous refuge has been overrun.
What strikes me most, though, is how little evidence we have ever demanded of one another.
I have sat through lectures of which I grasped perhaps a third, nodding at intervals, and was taken throughout for a man who followed.
We extend to anything with a face a generosity that we are now, quite reasonably, reluctant to extend to software.
The difficulty is that the generosity was never based on a test.
It was based on resemblance, and resemblance is exactly what has stopped being a reliable guide.

So perhaps the useful question is not whether a system really understands, which we cannot settle even for the person sitting next to us, but what it can safely be trusted with, which we can at least investigate.
That is a duller question, and I recommend it for that reason.
As for my neighbour, he became, I heard, a rather successful barrister.
I have no idea whether he understands the law.
His clients, sensibly, have never asked.

language_focus.explanation_es: El autor nunca sube la voz: *had the bad manners to set a question*, *with the satisfaction of the mediocre*, *I recommend it for that reason*. Dice menos de lo que piensa y deja que el lector complete la burla, también contra sí mismo.

*My own guess is…*, *I offer this tentatively*, *It may turn out to be…*, *A more honest approach might be…*: en el ensayo culto la opinión se presenta como hipótesis, y la cautela forma parte del argumento.

tasks.prompt: What is the writer's central claim?

options.text: That machines have at last been shown to understand language exactly as we do
That "real" understanding is harder to pin down than we assume
That memorising is useless
That examinations should be abolished

tasks.rationale_es: Parte de un caso sencillo y acaba mostrando que «entender de verdad» no es una sola cosa ni fácil de comprobar.

tasks.prompt: Match paragraphs 3, 5, 8 and 9 with the best heading. There is one extra heading.
tasks.rationale_es: El párrafo 3 propone la prueba del caso nuevo; el 5 cuenta el experimento mental; el 8 habla de tener algo en juego; el 9, de lo poco que nos exigimos entre personas.

options.text: He copied from the writer
He had a private tutor who told him the exam questions in advance
He matched stored solutions to question types
He disliked physics

tasks.rationale_es: No resolvía: reconocía el tipo de pregunta y recitaba la solución aprendida.

tasks.prompt: What does "with the satisfaction of the mediocre" suggest about the writer and his classmates?

options.text: They were pleased to see a better student fail
They were proud of their own excellent marks in the examination
They felt sorry for him
They understood physics deeply

tasks.rationale_es: Se incluye entre los mediocres: disfrutaron de la caída del que sacaba mejores notas.

tasks.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what is the mark of understanding?

options.text: Getting full marks
Coping correctly with cases never met before
Being able to recite a rule from memory without a single mistake
Working quickly

tasks.rationale_es: *To know how to go on*: saber seguir cuando el caso es nuevo.

tasks.prompt: The writer still regards the "unfamiliar case" test as a complete account of understanding.
tasks.rationale_es: *For most of my adult life I thought…*: ya no lo piensa.

tasks.prompt: Why do the machines pose a problem for that test?

options.text: They fail it completely
They are too expensive to test
They pass it, yet doubts remain
They refuse to answer questions that they have never seen before

tasks.rationale_es: Según la prueba deberían «entender», y aun así mucha gente siente que solo imitan.

tasks.prompt: In the thought experiment, what is the man in the room actually doing?

options.text: Translating letters
Learning the language little by little from the book of instructions
Writing to friends
Following rules about shapes he cannot read

tasks.rationale_es: Empareja formas siguiendo instrucciones; no entiende nada de lo que «escribe».

tasks.prompt: What is the writer's objection to the thought experiment?

options.text: It looks for understanding in a part rather than the whole
It is far too complicated for ordinary readers to follow properly
It was invented too long ago
It insults clerks

tasks.rationale_es: Tampoco una neurona entiende inglés: si hay comprensión, es del conjunto.

tasks.prompt: Why does the writer mention cyclists and physicists?

options.text: To suggest that scientists are, on the whole, rather impractical people in daily life
To recommend cycling
To show that different kinds of understanding can exist separately
To explain how a bicycle stays upright

tasks.rationale_es: Saber montar y saber explicar son cosas distintas que no siempre van juntas.

tasks.prompt: What does the writer mean by suggesting that understanding requires "a stake"?

options.text: Knowing involves being a creature that can be affected
Learning requires paying money
Machines need better hardware
People only learn what they are forced to learn at school

tasks.rationale_es: Entender que la estufa quema es, en parte, ser algo que se puede quemar.

tasks.prompt: How confident is the writer in his own suggestion?

options.text: Entirely certain
Cautious, and aware it may be self-serving
Indifferent
He presents it as established scientific fact, beyond all doubt

tasks.rationale_es: La ofrece con cautela y admite que puede ser el último refugio de una especie poco acostumbrada a competir.

tasks.prompt: The writer admits that he has appeared to follow lectures he did not fully understand.
tasks.rationale_es: Asentía de vez en cuando y lo tomaban por alguien que seguía la clase.

tasks.prompt: The writer has tested these systems himself in a laboratory.
tasks.rationale_es: Describe lo que hacen, pero no dice que los haya probado él.

tasks.prompt: What is implied by "His clients, sensibly, have never asked"?

options.text: His clients are foolish
In practice we judge by results, not by inner understanding
Barristers do not need to know any law at all in order to succeed
He lost touch with the writer

tasks.rationale_es: Remata la tesis: en la práctica nos basta con saber de qué podemos fiarnos.

tasks.prompt: Complete with one word from the text in each gap.
tasks.text: To have grasped a principle is to know how to {{1}} on. The writer offers his own guess {{2}}.
tasks.rationale_es: *Know how to go on* = saber seguir; *tentatively* = con cautela.
